KEY MESSAGE 1...Slowly improving weather overnight and Tuesday as 
the nor'easter weakens and moves away.

Although the low level swirl around the center of the nor'easter 
south of Long Island looks impressive on satellite imagery, the 
storm is quickly weakening as it's starting to move more quickly to 
the northeast. Still a good amount of moisture, wrapped around the 
circulation, producing a fairly large area of light rainfall. 
However as the dynamics weaken, the rainfall intensity is also on a 
downward trend. Expect most areas will see less than 1/2" of 
additional rainfall from this point forward. Models are all in good 
agreement in taking the low across the Cape overnight and then into 
the Gulf of Maine on Tuesday. Surface winds will slowly transition 
from NNE to NNW and then NW by Tuesday morning - except across our 
southern coastal waters and Nantucket, which will see winds go from 
the SE to SW and eventually W since the low center will pass north 
of those areas. Model forecast cross-sections indicate low level 
moisture will be slow to leave tomorrow, so expect a generally 
mostly cloudy day. Better chances for some afternoon sunshine will 
be across western areas. There is no blob of cold air that will come 
in behind the nor'easter, and in fact 925mb temperatures will be a 
little warmer than they were today. So given that and some breaks of 
sunshine, temperatures will be in the mid to upper 60s for most, and 
a few locations - especially in the CT River Valley - could hit
70F.

Also, given the downward trends in rainfall, have gone ahead and
cancelled the Flood Watch. Although some minor flooding is still
expected along portions of the Taunton River, we don't
anticipate any increase in risk for flooding across the area.  


KEY MESSAGE 2...Warm and Dry conditions arrive Wednesday through 
Friday followed by a chance for rainy and unsettled conditions this 
weekend. 

A mid-level ridge builds across the southeastern CONUS this week, 
while surface high pressure settles south of the region Wednesday 
through Friday, leading to a stretch of quieter and warmer weather. 
Guidance hints at a weak northern-stream shortwave Wednesday night 
into early Thursday, followed by a secondary shortwave Thursday 
night into Friday. PWATs Wednesday night into Thursday remain below 
1.2 inches and do not align particularly well with the best forcing. 
Outside of a brief light shower, would anticipate more clouds than 
anything. PWATs increase to around 1.5 inches Thursday night with 
the passage of the secondary weak shortwave, when a few light 
showers could brush the region. No significant impacts are 
anticipated with either disturbance. Temperatures trend warmer 
through the middle and latter half of the week, though the latest 
guidance has trended somewhat cooler compared to previous runs. 
Highs generally return to the lower and middle 70s, with Thursday 
potentially the warmest day as temperatures reach the middle to 
upper 70s. No notable cold is expected overnight, with lows 
generally falling into the 50s.

Forecast becomes a bit more interesting by late next week as a 
strong continental high pressure system arrives from SE Canada.
Guidance shows a rather sharp drop in temperatures with 850 
temps falling from +15-17C Friday to +4-6C on Saturday. Beyond 
this front, guidance is beginning to come into better agreement 
with depicting a strong area of low pressure across SE Canada on
Sunday. There remains a variety of solutions with the GFS/ICON 
depicting secondary cyclogenesis along a frontal boundary near 
the Carolinas and the ECMWF/CMC leaning more towards a strong 
frontal boundary. In any case, the second half of the weekend 
looks wet and unsettled. Behind this feature, guidance depicts a
much colder airmass moving in from Canada with 850mb temps 
falling below zero later Monday through Wednesday. These mid-
level temps would support highs in the 40s and 50s with 
nighttime lows possibly falling into the 30s depending on 
radiational cooling.
